question: What is drug distribution defined as in pharmacokinetics?

options.A: The permanent breakdown of active drug molecules in the liver
options.B: The reversible transfer of a drug between body compartments
options.C: The complete elimination of waste products through the kidneys
options.D: The rate at which a tablet dissolves in the stomach

explanation: Distribution refers to the reversible movement of a drug from the bloodstream into various tissues and body fluids. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why do fat-soluble drugs move quickly out of the bloodstream?

options.A: They repel water molecules in the body fluids
options.B: They bind tightly to blood proteins in the plasma
options.C: They easily cross the fatty cell membranes of tissues
options.D: They are actively pushed across blood vessel walls

explanation: Fat-soluble drugs easily cross cellular membranes because the membranes themselves are made of lipids. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which feature in standard blood vessels allows water-soluble drugs to leave the circulation?
explanation: Gaps or pores in standard capillary walls permit the passage of small water-soluble drug molecules. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h2)

question: What makes it hard for a drug to cross strict barriers in the body?

options.A: Small size and high fat solubility
options.B: Large size and high water solubility
options.C: Strong attraction to red blood cells

explanation: Large or water-soluble molecules cannot easily slip through tight cellular junctions without special transport. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which main blood protein is primarily responsible for binding acidic drugs?
explanation: Albumin is the main circulating plasma protein that binds acidic and neutral drug molecules in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does a very high volume of distribution tell you about a drug?

options.A: It binds permanently to red blood cells
options.B: It spreads heavily into body tissues
options.C: It leaves the body immediately through urine
options.D: It stays strictly inside the blood plasma

explanation: A high volume of distribution means the drug leaves the plasma and spreads extensively into body fat and other tissues. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h4)

question: Why might a doctor order a larger starting dose for a drug that spreads heavily into body tissues?

options.A: Most of the drug leaves the blood and goes into storage sites
options.B: Blood proteins destroy the drug before it works
options.C: The kidneys remove the entire dose too fast
options.D: The drug turns into crystals inside blood vessels

explanation: When a drug hides in tissues, a larger initial dose is needed to achieve effective therapeutic levels in the blood. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which group of organs receives a drug the fastest right after it enters the bloodstream?

options.B: Fat tissue and resting skeletal muscle

explanation: Organs with high blood flow receive more blood per minute, leading to rapid initial drug delivery. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h5)

question: Why do fat-soluble drugs tend to build up in body fat over time?

options.A: Fat tissue has low blood flow and stores fat-loving compounds well
options.B: Blood flow to fat is higher than to the brain
options.C: Fat cells pull drugs inward using active pumps
options.D: Fat tissue turns the drug into solid crystals

explanation: Adipose tissue acts as a slow-to-fill reservoir because of its low blood supply and affinity for fat-soluble compounds. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h5)

question: What feature of the blood-brain barrier stops water-soluble drugs from entering the brain?

options.D: Large gaps in the tissue walls

explanation: Tight junctions seal the gaps between endothelial cells in the brain, preventing water-soluble drugs from passing through. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is the main concern when a pregnant woman takes medications that cross the placenta?

options.A: Fetal metabolism destroys all drugs before they cause harm
options.B: Many fat-soluble drugs cross the placenta and can affect the fetus
options.C: Maternal proteins carry drugs only to the amniotic fluid
options.D: The placenta blocks all therapeutic drugs from the baby

explanation: The placenta is not an absolute barrier; fat-soluble drugs easily cross to the fetus and can cause adverse effects. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h6)

question: How does severe malnutrition affect how drugs behave in the body?

options.A: Dehydration greatly expands total body fluid volume
options.B: Infection permanently closes all blood vessel pores
options.C: Liver damage stops all fat-soluble drugs from entering body fat
options.D: Low blood protein levels increase the active, unbound part of the drug

explanation: Nutritional deficiencies lower albumin production, reducing binding sites and leaving more free drug to circulate. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h7)

question: A dehydrated child with severe diarrhea gets a standard dose of a water-soluble antibiotic. What is the likely result of having less fluid in the body?

options.A: Higher peak blood levels because the drug has less fluid space to spread into
options.B: Quick breakdown of the drug by high blood proteins
options.C: Lower blood levels because the drug is trapped in fat
options.D: Delayed absorption due to stopped digestion

explanation: A smaller fluid volume means the drug dilutes less, leading to higher initial blood concentrations and potential toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h7)

question: Why might a fat-soluble drug that spreads widely through the body stay active for a long time?

options.A: Cell membranes block the drug from reaching metabolic enzymes
options.B: Kidneys pull the drug back into the bloodstream
options.C: The drug slowly releases from fat tissue back into the blood
options.D: Blood proteins hold the drug too tightly for the liver to process

explanation: Fat and tissue reservoirs slowly leak stored drug back into circulation, keeping it in the body longer. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h8)

question: An older adult with changes in body fat is given a fat-soluble sedative. What should the nurse watch out for?

options.A: Longer sleepiness due to increased fat storage and slow release
options.B: Sudden kidney failure from fast urine elimination
options.C: Dehydration from a sudden increase in blood volume
options.D: Allergic skin rashes from liver breakdown

explanation: Older adults have a higher proportion of body fat, which increases storage space and lengthens the time fat-soluble drugs stay active. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h8)
